title: Inflation Is Catching Up to Wages — Are Americans Losing Buying Power?
summary: Economist explainer: wage growth is about to be overtaken by inflation, which would cut purchasing power, risk a wage-price spiral and push households deeper into debt.

assertions.quote: We are expeditiously close to the point where we will see the rate of change of inflation supersedes the average growth in wages.

verdicts.note: By mid-2026 real average hourly earnings turned negative year on year and stayed negative for six months.

Derived real average hourly earnings growth went from +1.2% in February 2026 to +0.1% in March, -0.2% in April and -0.8% in May as CPI inflation (3.3%, 3.8%, 4.2%) overtook nominal wage growth (3.4%, 3.6%, 3.3%).

assertions.quote: demand higher wages in order to keep up with those costs, which then lead companies to then increase prices further

verdicts.note: The mechanism exists, but post-2021 evidence shows spirals are rare when expectations stay anchored and labor bargaining power is weak.

assertions.quote: we are already seeing signs that this is happening with people having rising credit card debt

verdicts.note: Card balances and delinquencies rose in 2025-26, though rising balances partly reflect nominal growth rather than distress.

assertions.quote: the amount of credit card debt defaults that we've seen in the last year is reaching the same level that it did in 2008

verdicts.note: Card charge-off rates in 2025-26 approached 2008 levels but stayed below the 2009-10 peak above 10%.

assertions.quote: inflation in and of itself, if if it is controlled, is not inherently a bad thing if wages are able to keep up with it

verdicts.note: Real incomes determine living standards; 2% targets reflect that moderate, anticipated inflation has small costs.
